name: Cucuteni–Trypillia culture
info: The Cucuteni–Trypillia culture was a Neolithic–Chalcolithic farming culture of Moldova, north-eastern Romania and western Ukraine, c. 5050–2950 BCE, known for its painted pottery, its figurines, its burned and rebuilt settlements and its vast mega-sites.

facts.homeland: From the Carpathian Mountains to the Dniester and Dnieper, about 350,000 km², centred on present-day Moldova with large parts of western Ukraine and north-eastern Romania; its historical core on the middle to upper Dniester; key sites Cucuteni, Trypillia, Talianki, Poduri, Verteba Cave, Poiana Slatinei
facts.period: c. 5050–2950 BCE in all, in Early, Middle and Late periods; the Romanian scheme (Hubert Schmidt, 1932) runs Pre-Cucuteni I–III, Cucuteni A and B, then Horodiștea–Foltești, the Ukrainian (Tatiana Passek, 1949) Trypillia A, B and C; mega-sites in the middle phase, c. 4100–3500 BCE
facts.known: painted pottery with spiral designs, later fired in two-chamber kilns; clay figurines, many of them female; mega-sites of up to three thousand structures; settlements burned and rebuilt every 60–80 years; salt from springs, as at Poiana Slatinei; miniature wheeled models; the “Cucuteni Frumusica Dance”
facts.sources: Excavations at Cucuteni from 1885 (Teodor T. Burada and scholars from Iași) and at Kyiv and Trypillia from the 1890s (Vincenc Chvojka); about 3,000 sites known by 2003; geophysical surveys and the Collaborative Research Centre 1266 at Kiel University; isotope studies; ancient DNA from Verteba Cave and Moldova (Nikitin et al. 2010 and 2017, Mathieson et al. 2018, Immel et al. 2020); no writing

t: The culture spread from the eastern Carpathians to the Dnieper, and in its middle phase its people built some of the largest settlements in Eurasia, a few with as many as three thousand structures.
Its settlements were burned and rebuilt every 60 to 80 years, sometimes on the plan of the old buildings, for reasons scholars still debate.
How it ended is disputed: Marija Gimbutas saw invasion from the steppe, others gradual change or a drier climate, and ancient DNA shows steppe-related ancestry entering late in its history.
dyk: At Poduri in Romania thirteen habitation levels were built one on top of another over many years, as the settlement was destroyed and rebuilt on the same spot.
ev: The Cucuteni–Trypillia culture takes shape from earlier farming cultures in the region between the Prut and the Siret
In the middle phase mega-sites such as Talianki, with up to three thousand structures, are built
first half of the 4th millennium BCE
Miniature models of animals and cups on four wheels are made, showing that the idea of pulling things on wheels was known
The climate turns colder and drier, a change some scholars link to the culture’s end
The Cucuteni–Trypillia culture comes to an end, in circumstances still debated
Teodor T. Burada names and describes the culture after the village of Cucuteni in Romania
Vincenc Chvojka presents his Ukrainian finds to the 11th Congress of Archaeologists, the official date of the discovery of the Trypillia culture

sections.origins:
The culture was first named and described in 1884 by Teodor T. Burada, after Cucuteni, a village in Iași County in Romania, where he traced pottery fragments in road gravel back to their quarry; in 1885 he and other scholars from Iași began the first excavations there. At about the same time the Czech-born Ukrainian archaeologist Vincenc Chvojka found the first Ukrainian sites in Kyiv, presenting them in 1897, and finds made that year at Trypillia near Kyiv gave the culture its Ukrainian name. The finds of Romania, Ukraine and Moldova are now recognised as one cultural complex, called Cucuteni in Romania and Trypillia in Ukraine.

Its roots lie in the Starčevo–Körös–Criș and Vinča cultures, with influence from the Bug–Dniester culture and, in its early period, from the Linear Pottery culture to the north and the Boian culture to the south. Through colonisation and acculturation the formative Pre-Cucuteni/Trypillia A culture took shape, and during the 5th millennium BCE it spread from its homeland between the Prut and the Siret along the eastern foothills of the Carpathians to the plains of the Dnieper and Southern Bug. Europe was then at its warmest and wettest since the end of the last Ice Age, which favoured farming.

Its dating is contested: separate Romanian and Ukrainian schemes of phases are matched to radiocarbon dates in different ways. Ancient DNA shows people of mostly early European farmer ancestry, related to the Neolithic farmers of Anatolia, with some hunter-gatherer ancestry.
sections.society:
Most settlements were small and close together, 3 to 4 kilometres apart, in the valleys of the Siret, the Prut and the Dniester. In the middle phase, about 4100 to 3500 BCE, some grew into “mega-sites” with as many as three thousand structures, possibly home to 20,000 to 46,000 people, the largest settlements in Eurasia at the time; Talianki in Ukraine covered 335 hectares. Whether they were early cities is debated, and some scholars suggest they sheltered refugees. Houses were of wattle and daub, of logs or half underground, some two storeys tall, mostly with thatched roofs and clay-covered floors, and some were painted outside with swirling red designs.

People farmed with the ard, growing club wheat, oats, rye, proso millet, barley, peas and beans, and kept mostly cattle, with fewer pigs, sheep and goats; pictures of animals suggest that the ox was used for draught, and whether their horses were wild or domestic is unknown. Meat made up only about 10% of the diet in the large settlements, and a 2023 study found that cattle were pastured to manure the fields of pulses. Salt was boiled from springs, as at Poiana Slatinei, and a mega-site needed an estimated 36,000 to 100,000 kg a year.

Society has been proposed to have been egalitarian at first, and even in the largest settlements there is no evidence of labour specialisation. A 2024 study from Kiel University found that inequality was lower in the mega-sites, and that its return after several generations may explain their abandonment.
sections.beliefs:
Some settlements had a special building at their centre that archaeologists identify as a sanctuary, holding objects of clearly religious character, some deliberately buried in its floor, and such objects are also found in many houses. Most are clay figurines, which are believed to have been fetishes or charms that protected those who kept them. They are popularly called “goddesses”, though different figurines seem to have served different purposes. The “Cucuteni Frumusica Dance”, found in 1942 near Bodești, a stand formed of four stylised female figures in a ring, is thought to show a ritual dance, a hora. Marija Gimbutas based her theory of a peaceful, goddess-centred Old Europe partly on these figurines; her conclusions were always controversial and are now rejected by many scholars.

The burning of settlements every 60 to 80 years may itself have had a religious meaning. Some scholars suggest that each house was seen as an almost living being, sharing one circle of life with its pots, ovens and figurines, so that the settlement as a whole had a cycle of death and rebirth.

Burials are a puzzle: there are no Cucuteni cemeteries, and the Trypillia ones found are very late. The only Trypillian site where human remains of the first half of the 4th millennium BCE are found consistently is Verteba Cave in western Ukraine, skulls more often than other bones, and in the great majority of cases the dead were not laid to rest within the settlements.
sections.arts:
Pottery is the culture’s best-known work. Most was coiled by hand from local clay, though there is some evidence of a slow-turning potter’s wheel. Early pottery was smoky grey with raised and sunken relief; toward the end of the early period potters began to paint before firing, and white painting, taken from the Gumelnița–Karanovo culture, marks the start of the Cucuteni phase proper. Middle-period vessels carry spirals painted in black on yellow and red, and large pear-shaped jars held grain. Red came from iron oxide, black from iron magnetite, probably from Iacobeni in Romania, and manganese ore, probably from Nikopol in Ukraine, and white from calcium silicate. In the late period kilns with two chambers separated by a grate could reach 1,000–1,100 °C, though about 900 °C was usual, and a rope-like design replaced the spirals.

Clay figurines of women and animals and models of houses were made, and in the first half of the 4th millennium BCE miniature animals and cups on four wheels, often thought to be toys. They show the idea of pulling things on wheels, though there is no evidence yet of wheels on real wagons.

No textiles survive, but impressions on pottery show woven fabric and nalbinding, and clay weights suggest a warp-weighted loom. Tools were of flint, stone, bone, antler and horn and, later, copper. Weapons are rare, which implies a relatively peaceful culture.
sections.exchange:
Each household was largely self-sufficient, and trade rested at first on a few scarce minerals. The black pigment of the east of the culture’s area is not found in the west, suggesting that exchange across the whole area was limited. Salt had to be brought in bulk from the western Black Sea coast and the Carpathians, probably by river. Copper axes and tools were made from ore of Volyn and the Dnieper, and late in the culture copper from the Balkans and finished metal goods came from other peoples, followed at the very end by bronze.

The end of the culture is debated. From 1961 Marija Gimbutas argued that the people of the Kurgan culture, the Yamnaya and their forerunners of the Pontic–Caspian steppe, most likely speakers of Proto-Indo-European, destroyed it in a series of invasions; frequent evidence of violent death in Verteba Cave has been cited in support. J. P. Mallory, in 1989, pointed to Yamnaya settlements living for a time beside Cucuteni–Trypillia ones in the east, with open trade between them, and to refugees who abandoned 600–700 settlements for caves, islands and hilltops, and argued that a gradual transformation was possible. A third view links the end to the cold, dry climate that began around 3200 BCE, which would have favoured pastoralists, though the climate scheme behind it is not generally accepted.

Ancient DNA shows steppe-related ancestry entering the population in its late phase, perhaps as early as 3500 BCE, through long contact and gradual mixing.
sections.legacy:
Late in its history the culture’s area widened to the Volyn region, the Sluch and Horyn rivers and both banks of the Dnieper near Kyiv, with outlying communities on the Don and the Volga, and herding and horses grew in importance. On one view its trade network was supplanted by that of the Proto-Indo-European culture that replaced it, and in the Bronze Age Verteba Cave was used by successive waves of herders from the east, who mixed with the local descendants of the Trypillian population. Its farming may have helped create the open “cultural steppe” of the region today, as large populations turned woodland toward grassland.

The culture holds a large place in modern debate. Its figurines helped inspire Marija Gimbutas, Joseph Campbell and some late 20th-century feminists to propose a peaceful, egalitarian Old Europe overrun by warlike Indo-Europeans, a theory partly discredited by newer evidence of a more complex Neolithic society. Its mega-sites, as large as or perhaps larger than the city-states of Sumer and older by more than half a millennium, are central to arguments about early towns and inequality.

The largest collections are in museums in Russia, Ukraine and Romania, among them the Hermitage in St Petersburg and the Archaeology Museum Piatra Neamț. Excavation goes on: in 2026 a communal building of about 350 square metres, more than three times the size of the houses around it, was found at Stăuceni-Holm in north-eastern Romania.

summary: The Cucuteni–Trypillia culture was a farming culture of the lands between the Carpathians and the Dnieper from about 5050 to 2950 BCE. Its people made richly painted pottery and clay figurines, burned and rebuilt their settlements every few generations and, in its middle phase, built mega-sites among the largest of their time. Whether it ended by invasion, gradual change or climate is still debated.

Menotti, F. and Korvin-Piotrovsky, A. (eds.). The Tripolye Culture giant-settlements in Ukraine: Formation, Development and Decline. Oxford: Oxbow Books, 2012.
Ohlrau, René. Maidanets’ke: Development and decline of a Trypillia mega-site in Central Ukraine. Leiden: Sidestone Press, 2020.

notes: Dates conflict throughout the article. Kept the lead’s c. 5050–2950 BCE. The period headings give Early 5800–5000, Middle 5000–3500 and Late 3500–3000 BCE; the decline section gives 4800–2750 BCE; the economy section speaks of ‘2,750 years of its existence’ and copper arriving 3000–2750 BCE; Cucuteni A is quoted as 4600–4050. The lead also places the mega-sites both in ‘the 5th millennium BC’ and in the middle phase ‘c. 4100 to 3500 BC’; I used the latter.

Population: the lead says the mega-sites were ‘possibly inhabited by 20,000 to 46,000 people’ and the culture’s peak ‘may have reached or exceeded one million’; the economy section says ‘up to 15,000 people in the largest’ and Talianki had ‘a population of 15,000’. I gave the lead’s hedged figure once and Talianki’s area only; the million is left out.

Potter’s wheel: the lead claims the oldest potter’s wheel ever found (mid-5th millennium), but the middle-period section says the wheel ‘was not used yet’ and the pottery section speaks only of ‘some evidence’ of a slow wheel. I used the hedged wording and left out the ‘oldest’ claim. Likewise the lead’s ‘oldest evidence for wheeled vehicles’ is reduced to the models, which the article says are disputed evidence.

Copper: the economy section calls copper from 3000–2750 BCE the transition to the Eneolithic, but the Cărbuna copper hoard is dated to the beginning of the 5th millennium and Volyn ore is used in the middle period; I gave the facts without the transition claim.
Gimbutas: the article dates the steppe invasions both to ‘between 3000–2800 BC’ and to ‘beginning around 2500 BC’; I gave no date for them. Her 1961 article is named in the text.

Left out: the early-period division of labour by sex (stated without a source), the Cărbuna hoard and the stratification debate, Parpola’s wheeled-vehicle claim, the Diachenko and Nikitin refugee theories by name, the haplogroup lists and the 2022 blue-eye and lactose finding, the stature argument, and the garbled climate quotation.
Ohlrau’s title is printed “Maidanets'ke” in the article; I used a typographic apostrophe.
